Verify Now Blog > 12 PCB Layout Guidelines for Better Component Placement 12 PCB Layout Guidelines for Better Component Placement by: Mila Oct 29,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB Layout PCB Component Placement PCB Layout Guidelines PCB Design Guidelines PCB layout involves more than simply placing components and routing traces. Component spacing, decoupling capacitor placement, pad connections, thermal management, and manufacturing constraints all affect PCB assembly quality and long-term reliability. The following PCB layout guidelines cover 12 practical details that engineers should consider during PCB component placement and design. 1. SMT Component Spacing The spacing between surface-mount technology (SMT) components is an important consideration in PCB layout. Insufficient spacing can make solder paste printing and component placement more difficult, increase the risk of solder bridging, and complicate rework and maintenance. The following values can serve as preliminary references for PCB component spacing: Same-type components: A spacing of at least 0.3 mm may be used as a reference. Different types of components: A spacing of at least 0.13 × h + 0.3 mm may be used as a reference, where h is the maximum height difference between adjacent components. Components requiring manual placement or rework: A spacing of at least 1.5 mm may be considered, depending on the available working space and tools. These values are for reference only and are not universal manufacturing standards. Actual PCB component spacing should be determined based on component packages, pad dimensions, solder paste printing, placement equipment, and the manufacturing and assembly capabilities of the PCB supplier. 2. Spacing Between Through-Hole and SMT Components Adequate spacing should also be maintained between through-hole components and SMT components to prevent interference during component placement, soldering, and subsequent rework. A spacing of 1–3 mm can serve as a general reference, but the actual distance depends on component dimensions, lead positions, soldering methods, and maintenance requirements. For PCBs assembled using wave soldering, engineers should also consider component orientation, shadowing effects caused by adjacent components, and whether solder can reach the joints effectively. 3. IC Decoupling Capacitor Placement Decoupling capacitors should be placed as close as practical to the corresponding IC power pins. This helps shorten the current loop between the power supply and ground, reducing parasitic inductance and power supply noise. When an IC has multiple power pins, the number, capacitance, and placement of decoupling capacitors should be determined according to the datasheet, power distribution network, and actual current requirements. Where individual power pins require dedicated decoupling, the corresponding capacitors should be placed as close to those pins as possible. The grounding path is equally important. Keep the connections between the power pin, decoupling capacitor, and ground as short as practical. Unnecessarily long traces or excessive vias can reduce decoupling effectiveness, particularly at high frequencies. 4. Component Orientation and Clearance Near PCB Edges PCBs often undergo routing, V-scoring, or other depanelization processes. Components near PCB edges therefore require special attention to their orientation and clearance. First, consider the mechanical stress generated during depanelization. Ceramic capacitors, connectors, and other mechanically sensitive components should be positioned to minimize stress concentration at solder joints and component bodies. Component orientation should be determined by the depanelization method, pad geometry, and component characteristics rather than by a universal rule that all components must be parallel to the cutting direction. Second, sufficient component-free space should be maintained near PCB edges to prevent damage from cutting tools or depanelization equipment. The required clearance depends on the depanelization method, such as V-scoring, routing, or mouse bites, as well as component dimensions and the PCB manufacturer's capabilities. For components that are particularly sensitive to mechanical stress, consider using a depanelization method that reduces stress on the board and solder joints. 5. Connecting Adjacent PCB Pads When adjacent pads must be connected to the same net, the copper connections and trace widths should be planned carefully. Poorly designed copper connections may reduce the effective clearance between pads and increase the risk of solder bridging. During PCB layout, maintain adequate electrical clearance between pads and select trace widths according to current-carrying requirements. For fine-pitch components, pay particular attention to the relationship between pads, traces, and solder mask openings to avoid problems with solder paste printing and soldering quality. After completing the layout, run design rule checks (DRC) and verify that the design meets the PCB manufacturer's fabrication and assembly requirements. 6. Thermal Relief vs. Solid Copper Connections When a pad is connected to a copper plane, the connection method should be selected based on soldering requirements, current-carrying capacity, and thermal performance. Two common methods are thermal relief connections and solid copper connections. A thermal relief connection uses several narrow copper spokes to connect the pad to the surrounding copper plane. This reduces heat transfer from the pad into the larger copper area during soldering, making soldering and rework easier in many cases. A solid copper connection directly connects the pad to the copper plane. It generally provides lower electrical and thermal resistance, but the larger copper area can draw heat away from the pad, making it more difficult to reach the required soldering temperature. The appropriate method depends on current requirements, heat dissipation, soldering processes, and rework needs. For high-current or thermally demanding connections, do not reduce the number or width of copper spokes solely to make soldering easier without evaluating the electrical and thermal consequences. 7. Using Teardrops in PCB Layout When a trace connects to a pad or via through a narrow junction, a teardrop can be added where appropriate to create a smoother transition between the trace and the connection point. Teardrops offer several potential benefits: Improved connection reliability: They increase the copper area at the trace-to-pad junction, helping reduce the risk of a weakened or broken connection caused by drill misalignment, manufacturing tolerances, or mechanical stress. Enhanced mechanical robustness: The wider transition can make the connection less vulnerable to local narrowing or separation. Improved appearance: Teardrops create a smoother visual transition between traces and pads. However, teardrops are not necessary in every situation. For high-speed or impedance-sensitive traces, engineers should evaluate whether the resulting geometric changes could affect impedance continuity or signal integrity. 8. Trace Width at Component Pads During PCB layout, trace widths near component pads should be selected according to the electrical and mechanical requirements of the design. For differential signals, symmetrical analog circuits, and connections requiring balanced current distribution, trace symmetry, width matching, and length matching may be important for maintaining signal integrity and circuit performance. However, ordinary signal traces do not always need to have identical widths on both sides of a pad. Trace widths should be determined by current-carrying capacity, impedance requirements, pad dimensions, and manufacturing capabilities. Avoid unnecessary abrupt changes in trace width near pad connections. 9. Handling Unused IC Pins Unused IC pins must be handled according to the device datasheet and application requirements. They should not all be connected to ground or left floating indiscriminately. For example: NC pins: Follow the datasheet instructions. Some pins must remain unconnected and should not be grounded without authorization. Unused input pins: Connect them to the specified logic level or use the recommended pull-up, pull-down, or other biasing method to prevent undefined input states. Unused output pins: Do not connect them directly to ground or a power rail unless the datasheet explicitly permits it. Pins permitted to float: Leave them unconnected only when this is allowed or required by the device documentation. For physical pins that are present on the IC but not used in the application, ensure that the PCB footprint correctly represents the actual package. Whether the corresponding pads should be connected to ground or handled in another way depends on the pin function and the device manufacturer's recommendations. Adding a pad and connecting it to ground does not necessarily provide effective shielding. An incorrect connection may instead cause a short circuit or interfere with normal device operation. 10. Via-in-Pad Design Considerations During PCB layout, placing a conventional open via directly within a pad can cause solder to flow into the hole during assembly. This may result in insufficient solder at the joint, poor soldering quality, or other assembly defects. For ordinary SMT pads, avoid placing untreated open vias directly within the pads, particularly for fine-pitch components, unless the manufacturing process supports the design. However, vias are not universally prohibited within pads. Via-in-pad is a common design approach for packages such as BGAs, where routing density and electrical performance may require it. Depending on the application, via filling, capping, or other appropriate via treatments may be needed to prevent solder loss and ensure reliable assembly. Select the appropriate approach based on the component package, via structure, and PCB manufacturer's process capabilities. 11. PCB Edge Clearance for Traces, Pads, and Components Copper traces, pads, and components should maintain adequate clearance from PCB edges to prevent damage during fabrication, depanelization, and subsequent assembly. If copper features or pads are too close to the board edge, routing, V-scoring, or other depanelization processes may damage the copper, expose conductors, or compromise electrical reliability. For single-sided boards and substrates with relatively low mechanical strength, additional attention should be paid to structural integrity and component placement near the edges. The required PCB edge clearance should be determined according to the board material, thickness, depanelization method, and manufacturer's capabilities. Include these clearances in the PCB design rules and verify them before manufacturing. 12. Keep Electrolytic Capacitors Away from Heat Sources Electrolytic capacitors are sensitive to operating temperature. Prolonged exposure to elevated temperatures can accelerate electrolyte loss and shorten capacitor service life. During PCB layout, avoid placing electrolytic capacitors too close to power resistors, power semiconductors, transformers, or other heat-generating components whenever possible. If close placement is unavoidable, evaluate the thermal impact based on component temperature rise, airflow direction, and the actual operating environment. Also consider the capacitor's rated operating temperature, ripple current, and self-heating to ensure that it operates within acceptable limits under real-world conditions. Distance from a heat source alone is not sufficient to determine whether a capacitor is safe. Thermal design and the operating conditions of the complete product must also be considered. Conclusion PCB layout affects not only electrical performance but also manufacturability, soldering quality, and long-term reliability. In addition to routing and component placement, engineers should consider assembly processes, mechanical stress, thermal requirements, and the recommendations provided in component datasheets. After completing the PCB design, perform design rule checks and verify the layout against the PCB manufacturer's capabilities and assembly requirements. Careful attention to these PCB layout guidelines can help reduce design issues and improve PCB fabrication and assembly reliability Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Improved appearance: Teardrops create a smoother visual transition between traces and pads. However, teardrops are not necessary in every situation. For high-speed or impedance-sensitive traces, engineers should evaluate whether the resulting geometric changes could affect impedance continuity or signal integrity. 8. Trace Width at Component Pads During PCB layout, trace widths near component pads should be selected according to the electrical and mechanical requirements of the design. For differential signals, symmetrical analog circuits, and connections requiring balanced current distribution, trace symmetry, width matching, and length matching may be important for maintaining signal integrity and circuit performance. However, ordinary signal traces do not always need to have identical widths on both sides of a pad. Trace widths should be determined by current-carrying capacity, impedance requirements, pad dimensions, and manufacturing capabilities. Avoid unnecessary abrupt changes in trace width near pad connections. 9. Handling Unused IC Pins Unused IC pins must be handled according to the device datasheet and application requirements. They should not all be connected to ground or left floating indiscriminately. For example: NC pins: Follow the datasheet instructions. Some pins must remain unconnected and should not be grounded without authorization. Unused input pins: Connect them to the specified logic level or use the recommended pull-up, pull-down, or other biasing method to prevent undefined input states. Unused output pins: Do not connect them directly to ground or a power rail unless the datasheet explicitly permits it. Pins permitted to float: Leave them unconnected only when this is allowed or required by the device documentation. For physical pins that are present on the IC but not used in the application, ensure that the PCB footprint correctly represents the actual package. Whether the corresponding pads should be connected to ground or handled in another way depends on the pin function and the device manufacturer's recommendations. Adding a pad and connecting it to ground does not necessarily provide effective shielding. An incorrect connection may instead cause a short circuit or interfere with normal device operation. 10. Via-in-Pad Design Considerations During PCB layout, placing a conventional open via directly within a pad can cause solder to flow into the hole during assembly. This may result in insufficient solder at the joint, poor soldering quality, or other assembly defects. For ordinary SMT pads, avoid placing untreated open vias directly within the pads, particularly for fine-pitch components, unless the manufacturing process supports the design. However, vias are not universally prohibited within pads. Via-in-pad is a common design approach for packages such as BGAs, where routing density and electrical performance may require it. Depending on the application, via filling, capping, or other appropriate via treatments may be needed to prevent solder loss and ensure reliable assembly. Select the appropriate approach based on the component package, via structure, and PCB manufacturer's process capabilities. 11. PCB Edge Clearance for Traces, Pads, and Components Copper traces, pads, and components should maintain adequate clearance from PCB edges to prevent damage during fabrication, depanelization, and subsequent assembly. If copper features or pads are too close to the board edge, routing, V-scoring, or other depanelization processes may damage the copper, expose conductors, or compromise electrical reliability. For single-sided boards and substrates with relatively low mechanical strength, additional attention should be paid to structural integrity and component placement near the edges. The required PCB edge clearance should be determined according to the board material, thickness, depanelization method, and manufacturer's capabilities. Include these clearances in the PCB design rules and verify them before manufacturing. 12. Keep Electrolytic Capacitors Away from Heat Sources Electrolytic capacitors are sensitive to operating temperature. Prolonged exposure to elevated temperatures can accelerate electrolyte loss and shorten capacitor service life. During PCB layout, avoid placing electrolytic capacitors too close to power resistors, power semiconductors, transformers, or other heat-generating components whenever possible. If close placement is unavoidable, evaluate the thermal impact based on component temperature rise, airflow direction, and the actual operating environment. Also consider the capacitor's rated operating temperature, ripple current, and self-heating to ensure that it operates within acceptable limits under real-world conditions. Distance from a heat source alone is not sufficient to determine whether a capacitor is safe. Thermal design and the operating conditions of the complete product must also be considered. Conclusion PCB layout affects not only electrical performance but also manufacturability, soldering quality, and long-term reliability. In addition to routing and component placement, engineers should consider assembly processes, mechanical stress, thermal requirements, and the recommendations provided in component datasheets. After completing the PCB design, perform design rule checks and verify the layout against the PCB manufacturer's capabilities and assembly requirements. Careful attention to these PCB layout guidelines can help reduce design issues and improve PCB fabrication and assembly reliability Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > Clock Circuit Design Guidelines for PCB Layout Clock Circuit Design Guidelines for PCB Layout by: Mila Nov 06,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout clock circuit crystal oscillator pcb Layout pcb clock signal routing Clock circuits play an essential role in electronic systems by providing timing signals that synchronize the operation of different components. However, improper clock circuit design can lead to signal interference, timing errors, and system instability. This article explores the PCB design guidelines for crystal circuits, active oscillators, and clock distributors, covering key considerations for component placement, signal routing, and noise reduction. 1. Crystal A clock is an essential part of any electronic system. It acts like the heartbeat of the system, providing synchronization signals to different components. If the clock signal becomes unstable or fails, the entire system may malfunction or stop working. Therefore, proper clock circuit design is essential in PCB design. Common clock sources and distribution components used in PCBs include crystals, oscillators, and clock distributors. Some ICs may generate their own clock signals internally. However, the clock signal ultimately originates from a crystal, an oscillator, or another clock source before being distributed to other components. When designing a crystal circuit, consider the following guidelines: Place the crystal as close as possible to the IC's oscillator pins to minimize trace length and reduce external interference. For designs with high electromagnetic compatibility requirements, consider using a crystal with a metal shield package. Ensure that the shield is properly grounded according to the component datasheet. Avoid routing other signal traces beneath the crystal and its load capacitors, especially high-speed digital signals. A continuous GND reference plane can be provided beneath the crystal circuit according to the IC manufacturer's layout recommendations. Keep high-speed digital signal traces away from the crystal to reduce crosstalk. Keep the ground connections of the load capacitors as short as possible to minimize parasitic inductance and provide a low-impedance return path. A GND guard area can be added around the crystal according to the recommended layout. If necessary, use GND vias to connect the ground copper on different layers. Place the crystal and its two load capacitors close to the IC's oscillator pins. Follow the component manufacturer's reference design for the exact placement arrangement. Common crystal packages used in PCB design include 2-pin through-hole packages, 2-pin SMD packages, and 4-pin SMD packages. （Common crystal package types） Although crystals are available in different package sizes and specifications, their basic operating principles and peripheral circuit designs are similar. Therefore, many PCB placement and routing guidelines are applicable across different crystal designs. A basic crystal circuit is shown below: （Basic crystal circuit schematic） The two capacitors shown in the schematic are load capacitors. They connect the two crystal terminals to ground and provide the required load capacitance for stable oscillation. Their values should be determined based on the crystal datasheet, the IC's internal oscillator characteristics, and the parasitic capacitance of the PCB. 2. Crystal Circuit Placement and Routing When placing a crystal circuit, position the two load capacitors as close as possible to the crystal and the IC's oscillator pins. This helps minimize trace length and reduce the impact of parasitic parameters. The placement is shown below: （Crystal circuit placement） When routing the crystal circuit, keep the two connections between the crystal and the IC as short as possible and preferably close to each other to reduce parasitic capacitance and external interference. Note that these two traces are not true differential signal lines, so differential routing rules should not be applied directly. Avoid unnecessary vias and follow the IC manufacturer's layout recommendations to determine whether GND guard traces are needed. The routing layout is shown below: （Crystal circuit routing） 3. Crystal Circuit Design Variations The circuit described above is the most basic and commonly used crystal circuit design. In practical PCB designs, additional components such as series resistors and test points may be included to meet debugging or signal integrity requirements. However, the basic design principles remain the same. Based on the guidelines above, consider the following points when placing components: （Crystal circuit layout with a series resistor and test point） Place the crystal, associated capacitors, and series resistor on the same PCB layer whenever possible to reduce vias and shorten connection paths. If test points are required, avoid long stubs. Additional trace branches may introduce parasitic capacitance and affect oscillator stability. Avoid placing high-power components near the crystal, such as power ICs, MOSFETs, and inductors, as heat generated by these components may affect crystal frequency stability. Routing guidelines: Place and route the crystal on the same layer as the IC whenever possible to minimize vias. If layer changes are necessary, ensure a continuous return path and add nearby GND vias when needed. Keep crystal traces as short as possible. Trace width should be determined based on the IC manufacturer's recommendations and PCB fabrication capabilities rather than increased unnecessarily. GND guard traces can be added around the crystal circuit when appropriate. Connect them to the reference ground plane using GND vias. Keep the crystal circuit area relatively isolated. Avoid routing other high-speed signals through this area to reduce crosstalk and external noise interference. 4. Oscillator Circuit Design Unlike passive crystals, active oscillators integrate an internal oscillation circuit and can directly output clock signals. An active oscillator circuit typically consists of an oscillator device, a power supply decoupling circuit, and an optional source-series resistor selected according to the output interface and load requirements. A typical oscillator circuit is shown below: （Active oscillator circuit schematic） The PCB placement and routing layout is shown below: （Active oscillator PCB layout and routing） Placement and routing guidelines: Place power decoupling capacitors as close as possible to the oscillator's power supply pins. Prioritize a short power and ground loop for the high-frequency decoupling capacitor. If multiple decoupling capacitors are used, select their capacitance values and placement based on the component datasheet and power integrity requirements. There is no need to mechanically follow a fixed large-to-small capacitor arrangement. Determine whether a source-series resistor is needed based on the oscillator's output type, drive capability, trace length, and load conditions. If required, place it as close as possible to the oscillator output pin. Determine the clock signal impedance based on the oscillator output interface, receiver requirements, and PCB stackup. For clock signals that require transmission line control, implement appropriate impedance design. For long clock traces, consider routing them on an inner layer while maintaining a continuous reference plane. If layer transitions are necessary, add nearby GND return vias when appropriate. Maintain adequate spacing between clock traces and other signal traces to reduce crosstalk. The required spacing depends on signal edge rate, trace length, and layer-to-layer coupling. For longer clock traces, GND guard traces may be used when appropriate. Ensure that the guard traces are properly grounded and do not compromise signal integrity. 5. Clock Distributor Design A clock distributor is primarily used to distribute a clock signal from a clock source to multiple ICs or functional modules. Different clock distributors vary in terms of output count, frequency range, output interface, and drive capability. During PCB design, carefully plan the placement of the clock distributor relative to the receiving ICs to minimize clock signal routing distances. For designs that require clock skew control, also consider the routing lengths and loads of different output channels. The clock distributor is often placed at a relatively central position among the receiving devices. A typical clock distributor circuit is shown below: （Clock distributor circuit schematic） The PCB layout is shown below: （Clock distributor PCB layout） Placement and routing guidelines: Place the clock generation circuit as close as possible to the clock distributor. Common clock sources include crystals, active oscillators, and other clock generation circuits. Position the clock distributor appropriately in relation to the receiving ICs to minimize clock signal routing distances. For designs requiring clock skew control, keep the routing lengths and loads of related clock output paths as consistent as possible. Avoid placing high-power components near the clock distributor, such as power ICs, MOSFETs, and inductors, as temperature variations may affect clock performance. For long clock signal traces, consider routing them on inner layers while maintaining a continuous reference plane. If layer transitions are necessary, add GND return vias close to the signal vias to provide a continuous return path. Control trace impedance and signal spacing according to the clock frequency, edge rate, and interface requirements to reduce crosstalk and signal reflections. A well-designed clock circuit is essential for maintaining stable and reliable operation in electronic systems. Whether using a crystal, an active oscillator, or a clock distributor, careful component placement, short signal paths, proper grounding, and appropriate impedance control all contribute to better clock signal integrity. By following these PCB clock circuit design guidelines, engineers can reduce noise interference, minimize signal distortion, and improve overall system stability. Verify Now Blog > Differential Pair Routing: 3 Common Design Mistakes to Avoid Differential Pair Routing: 3 Common Design Mistakes to Avoid by: Mila Nov 04,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout Differential Pair Differential Pair Routing High-Speed PCB Design Differential Pair Routing In high-speed PCB design , differential pairs are increasingly used, especially in high-speed interfaces such as USB, HDMI, and PCIe. These interfaces commonly use differential signaling for reliable data transmission. Why is differential signaling so widely used? Compared with conventional single-ended routing, differential pairs offer better noise immunity, help suppress common-mode noise and electromagnetic interference (EMI), and improve signal integrity and timing performance. Differential Pair Routing Requirements In PCB design, a differential pair consists of two closely coupled signal traces. To ensure signal transmission quality, these traces generally need to have matched lengths, equal widths, consistent spacing, and symmetrical routing. Differential impedance must also be controlled according to the design requirements. （Differential Pair Routing Requirements） 1. Equal Length Equal length means keeping the two traces in a differential pair as close in length as possible. The purpose is to control the propagation delay difference (skew) between the two signals, maintain proper timing alignment, and reduce signal imbalance and the resulting common-mode noise. 2. Equal Width and Spacing Equal width means maintaining the same trace width for both signals. Equal spacing means keeping the distance between the two traces as consistent as possible, allowing them to run symmetrically and in parallel. This helps maintain a stable coupling relationship between the two traces, minimizes differential impedance variations, and improves signal transmission quality. 3. It is also important to minimize impedance variations along the routing path. Differential impedance is affected by several factors, including trace width, spacing between the two traces, copper thickness, PCB material, and stackup structure. These factors should all be considered during the design process to maintain consistent differential impedance. 4. Verify Now Blog > PCB Copper Thickness Guide for Current, Impedance, and Heat Dissipation PCB Copper Thickness Guide for Current, Impedance, and Heat Dissipation by: Mila Oct 26,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB copper thickness PCB copper weight PCB copper thickness selection PCB copper thickness for current PCB copper thickness affects current-carrying capacity, trace impedance, heat dissipation, and manufacturing complexity. Thicker copper is not always better, and thinner copper is not always the right choice for high-density designs. Choosing the right PCB copper thickness requires balancing current requirements, signal frequency, routing density, and PCB manufacturing capabilities. （PCB current path） Why Are Different PCB Copper Thicknesses Used? PCB copper thickness is commonly specified by copper weight in ounces (oz), which represents the weight of copper per unit area. For standard PCB copper foil, 1 oz is approximately 35 μm thick, 2 oz is approximately 70 μm, 3 oz is approximately 105 μm, and 0.5 oz is approximately 17.5 μm. These are approximate conversions, and the actual copper thickness depends on the manufacturing process and specified requirements. Current-Carrying Capacity Thicker copper generally provides a larger conductor cross-sectional area and lower resistance, helping reduce voltage drop and resistive heating. Under otherwise similar conditions, increasing copper thickness can improve a trace's current-carrying capacity. 0.5 oz (approximately 17.5 μm): Suitable for some high-density PCBs, fine signal traces, and low-current circuits. 1 oz (approximately 35 μm): A common general-purpose copper weight for many digital circuits and power designs. 2 oz (approximately 70 μm): Suitable for industrial control boards, power supply boards, and power circuits with higher current requirements. 3 oz and above (approximately 105 μm and above): Used in power electronics, renewable energy equipment, and other high-current applications. However, current-carrying capacity depends on more than copper thickness. Trace width, allowable temperature rise, whether the trace is on an inner or outer layer, ambient temperature, and heat dissipation conditions also matter. Copper thickness alone cannot determine how much current a PCB trace can safely carry. For high-current designs, increasing copper thickness is an alternative to widening traces, but both options should be evaluated against the actual current and temperature-rise requirements. Impact on Impedance Control In high-speed digital and RF PCB designs , copper thickness is one of the factors that affect trace impedance. With the dielectric thickness, dielectric constant, reference plane, and target impedance held constant, changes in copper thickness can affect trace impedance and the required trace width. For microstrip traces, increasing copper thickness changes the field distribution and must be accounted for when calculating the required width. Existing impedance parameters should not be reused without verification. Thinner copper, such as 0.5 oz: Generally more suitable for fine traces and high-density routing, including certain HDI and BGA fan-out designs. Thicker copper, such as 2 oz or 3 oz: May require wider traces to achieve the same target impedance, consuming more routing space. High-frequency signal loss is also affected by copper surface roughness, dielectric loss, and trace geometry. Surface roughness is not determined by copper thickness alone. High-speed and RF designs should therefore consider copper thickness, copper foil type, stackup, and impedance requirements together rather than simply increasing or decreasing copper thickness. Impact on Heat Dissipation Copper has good thermal conductivity. Increasing copper thickness can improve in-plane heat conduction within copper layers and reduce resistive losses in traces and copper planes. In power supply boards and power circuits, using 2 oz or 3 oz copper can help improve current handling and heat spreading. However, actual thermal performance also depends on copper area, thermal vias, PCB layer structure, component packages, and the overall thermal path. Thicker copper can be part of a thermal management strategy, but it does not replace proper copper plane design, thermal vias, and an effective heat dissipation structure. PCB Manufacturing and Trace Width/Spacing Limitations Copper thickness also affects PCB manufacturing complexity. Thinner copper, such as 0.5 oz: Generally more suitable for fine traces and smaller trace widths and spacing, supporting high-density BGA fan-out and HDI designs. Thicker copper, such as 2 oz or 3 oz: Requires greater attention to etch undercut and trace cross-sectional control, making fine-line fabrication more challenging. For example, a PCB with 3 oz copper generally cannot use the same fine-line design rules as a standard thin-copper board without checking manufacturing feasibility. Whether 3–4 mil (approximately 0.076–0.102 mm) traces are achievable depends on the copper thickness, finished copper requirements, and the PCB manufacturer's process capabilities. During PCB design, confirm the manufacturer's minimum trace width and spacing requirements to avoid design-for-manufacturing (DFM) issues or additional fabrication costs. Cost and Weight Thicker copper generally requires more copper material and may increase the complexity of etching and trace formation. As a result, manufacturing costs and PCB weight may increase. For consumer electronics and conventional digital circuits, 1 oz copper is often sufficient when it meets current, impedance, and temperature-rise requirements. Choosing thicker copper without a clear engineering need can increase cost without providing a meaningful benefit. PCB Copper Thickness Chart and Common Applications The following PCB copper thickness chart summarizes common copper weights, approximate thicknesses, and typical applications. These applications are examples rather than fixed selection rules. The appropriate PCB copper thickness depends on current requirements, allowable temperature rise, impedance targets, manufacturing capabilities, and cost. Inner and outer layers can also use different copper thicknesses. For example, a design may use 2 oz copper on the outer layers and 1 oz on the inner layers. The suitability of this configuration depends on the stackup, impedance requirements, and the manufacturer's capabilities. Common PCB Copper Thickness Design Mistakes 1. Increasing trace width without considering copper thickness and temperature rise Both trace width and copper thickness affect conductor cross-sectional area and resistance. For high-current circuits, evaluate trace width, copper thickness, and allowable temperature rise together rather than adjusting only one parameter. 2. Using thick copper indiscriminately for high-speed PCBs Changes in copper thickness can affect trace impedance and available routing space. High-speed digital and RF designs should account for stackup, target impedance, and copper foil characteristics, with impedance calculations or simulations used for verification where appropriate. 3. Using excessively small trace widths and spacing on thick-copper boards Thick copper makes etching and trace formation more challenging. Check the manufacturer's minimum trace width and spacing for the specified copper thickness, and consult the fabricator when necessary. 4. Confusing base copper thickness with finished copper thickness Base copper thickness and finished copper thickness are not necessarily the same. In common PCB manufacturing processes, outer layers may undergo pattern plating, which adds copper. Therefore, 1 oz base copper does not mean that every area of the finished PCB will be exactly 35 μm thick. When specifying copper thickness, confirm whether the requirement refers to base copper or finished copper, and define the required thickness for inner and outer layers according to the manufacturing process. Conclusion Choosing the right PCB copper thickness requires balancing current-carrying capacity, impedance control, heat dissipation, routing density, and manufacturing cost. A 0.5 oz copper weight may be suitable for certain fine-line designs, 1 oz is a common general-purpose option, and 2 oz or 3 oz and above can be considered for power circuits with higher current and thermal requirements. For high-current designs, evaluate trace width, copper thickness, and temperature rise together. For high-speed and RF designs, consider impedance, stackup, and copper foil characteristics. The final selection should also account for the PCBWay manufacturer's process capabilities to ensure that the design meets both performance and manufacturability requirements. Inner and outer layers can also use different copper thicknesses. For example, a design may use 2 oz copper on the outer layers and 1 oz on the inner layers. The suitability of this configuration depends on the stackup, impedance requirements, and the manufacturer's capabilities. Common PCB Copper Thickness Design Mistakes 1. Increasing trace width without considering copper thickness and temperature rise Both trace width and copper thickness affect conductor cross-sectional area and resistance. For high-current circuits, evaluate trace width, copper thickness, and allowable temperature rise together rather than adjusting only one parameter. 2. Using thick copper indiscriminately for high-speed PCBs Changes in copper thickness can affect trace impedance and available routing space. High-speed digital and RF designs should account for stackup, target impedance, and copper foil characteristics, with impedance calculations or simulations used for verification where appropriate. 3. Using excessively small trace widths and spacing on thick-copper boards Thick copper makes etching and trace formation more challenging. Check the manufacturer's minimum trace width and spacing for the specified copper thickness, and consult the fabricator when necessary. 4. Confusing base copper thickness with finished copper thickness Base copper thickness and finished copper thickness are not necessarily the same. In common PCB manufacturing processes, outer layers may undergo pattern plating, which adds copper. Therefore, 1 oz base copper does not mean that every area of the finished PCB will be exactly 35 μm thick. When specifying copper thickness, confirm whether the requirement refers to base copper or finished copper, and define the required thickness for inner and outer layers according to the manufacturing process. Conclusion Choosing the right PCB copper thickness requires balancing current-carrying capacity, impedance control, heat dissipation, routing density, and manufacturing cost. A 0.5 oz copper weight may be suitable for certain fine-line designs, 1 oz is a common general-purpose option, and 2 oz or 3 oz and above can be considered for power circuits with higher current and thermal requirements. For high-current designs, evaluate trace width, copper thickness, and temperature rise together. For high-speed and RF designs, consider impedance, stackup, and copper foil characteristics. The final selection should also account for the PCBWay manufacturer's process capabilities to ensure that the design meets both performance and manufacturability requirements. Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Considerations for Single-Point and Multi-Point Grounding PCB Layout Considerations for Single-Point and Multi-Point Grounding by: Mila Oct 27,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB Layout single point grounding Single-Point and Multi-Point Grounding PCB grounding is an important part of PCB layout , affecting circuit stability, noise levels, signal integrity, and electromagnetic compatibility (EMC). Different circuits have different grounding requirements, and single-point grounding, multi-point grounding, and mixed grounding each have their own applications. This article explains the differences between these grounding techniques and highlights key considerations for effective PCB grounding. 1. Basic Principles of PCB Grounding In a PCB, ground provides a voltage reference for the circuit and a return path for current. Ideally, the ground plane should have low impedance. However, copper traces, vias, and connection structures introduce parasitic resistance and inductance. As frequency increases, parasitic inductance generally has a greater impact on grounding impedance. Therefore, PCB grounding design should consider not only DC resistance but also signal frequency, return paths, and reference-plane continuity. Key considerations include: Minimize grounding impedance: Use ground planes, copper pours, and vias appropriately to reduce unnecessary impedance along grounding paths. Control noise coupling: Arrange sensitive analog circuits, digital circuits, and power circuits to minimize interference. Maintain continuous return paths: For high-speed signals, avoid reference-plane splits and other structures that force return currents to take detours. Choose an appropriate grounding technique: No single grounding method is suitable for every PCB layout. 2. Three Common PCB Grounding Techniques （Single-Point vs. Multi-Point Grounding in PCB Design） Single-Point Grounding Single-point grounding connects multiple circuit grounds at a designated point to help reduce common-impedance coupling between circuit sections. This technique is often used in low-frequency analog circuits, sensor circuits, and other applications where coupling through shared ground paths is a concern. Key design considerations include: Choose the connection point carefully: Avoid routing large return currents through ground paths shared with sensitive analog circuits. Keep grounding paths short: Minimize unnecessary detours while maintaining appropriate electrical connections. Consider high-frequency behavior: Single-point grounding is not always suitable for high-frequency circuits, as long grounding wires can introduce additional inductance. Multi-Point Grounding Multi-point grounding connects a circuit ground to a ground plane or grounding structure at multiple locations. This approach can shorten grounding paths and reduce impedance at high frequencies. It is commonly used in high-speed digital circuits, RF circuits, and designs that require low-impedance high-frequency return paths. Key design considerations include: Prioritize ground-plane continuity: Provide a stable reference path for signals, especially high-speed signals. Place ground vias appropriately: Add vias near connectors, shielding structures, and other locations where they help shorten return paths. Avoid unnecessary return-path detours: Check whether ground-plane slots, splits, or poorly planned connections could interrupt return currents. More ground vias do not automatically result in better grounding. Their placement and the overall return-path structure are equally important. Mixed Grounding Mixed grounding combines different grounding strategies according to the requirements of individual circuit sections. For example, a low-frequency sensitive analog circuit may use a designated single-point connection, while a high-speed digital circuit relies on a continuous ground plane and multiple grounding connections. This approach is useful for mixed-signal PCBs and complex systems with different frequency and current requirements. Key design considerations include: Separate circuit functions through layout: Arrange analog and digital components appropriately and route signals to reduce noise coupling. Evaluate ground separation carefully: Do not assume that all mixed-signal circuits require split ground planes. Plan return paths across circuit sections: If a split ground plane is necessary, ensure that signals crossing between sections have appropriate return paths. Comparison of PCB Grounding Techniques 3. PCB Grounding Guidelines for Single-Point and Multi-Point Grounding Single-Point Grounding Guidelines The main goal of single-point grounding is to control common impedance and prevent current from one circuit section from interfering with another through a shared grounding path. Plan ground connections carefully: Avoid routing large return currents through grounding paths shared with sensitive analog circuits. Minimize unnecessary path lengths: Reduce detours while maintaining appropriate circuit connections. Consider high-frequency performance: Do not select single-point grounding solely based on the number of circuit sections. Its suitability depends on the frequency range and circuit characteristics. Multi-Point Grounding Guidelines The main goal of multi-point grounding is to provide low-impedance, continuous return paths for current. Maintain ground-plane continuity: For high-speed signals, avoid routing across split reference-plane regions. Place ground vias strategically: Position vias near connectors, shielding structures, and other locations where they improve return-path continuity. The exact placement depends on the circuit and PCB structure. Minimize return-path detours: Check whether ground-plane slots, splits, or reference-layer changes could affect the return paths of critical signals. 4. Grounding Design for Mixed-Signal PCBs Mixed-signal PCBs contain both analog and digital circuits. Digital switching can generate transient currents, while analog circuits may be sensitive to small amounts of noise. The goal is to control noise coupling and provide appropriate return paths for different signals. Arrange Components into Functional Zones Arrange analog circuits, digital circuits, and switching power supplies according to their functions. Keep sensitive analog signal paths short and avoid routing high-speed digital signals through sensitive analog areas. For switching power supplies, pay particular attention to switching nodes and high-frequency current loops. Avoid placing these noisy areas close to sensitive analog circuits whenever possible. Handle AGND and DGND Carefully AGND and DGND refer to analog ground and digital ground, respectively. However, this does not mean that every PCB must separate them into two independent ground planes. For many mixed-signal circuits, a continuous ground plane combined with careful component placement, signal routing, and current-path management is a sensible starting point. If an IC datasheet specifies that AGND and DGND must be connected at a particular location, follow the manufacturer's recommendations. When using a 0-ohm resistor, ferrite bead, or another component to connect separate ground nets, evaluate its impedance and noise effects for the specific circuit rather than treating it as a universal solution. Maintain Continuous Signal Return Paths For high-speed signals, return current typically flows in the reference plane near the signal trace. If a trace crosses a ground-plane split, slot, or reference-layer transition, the return current may be forced to take a longer path. This can increase loop area and electromagnetic interference (EMI). Therefore, PCB layout should provide continuous reference planes for critical high-speed signals whenever possible. When a signal changes reference layers, verify that its return path remains adequately connected. （Mixed-Signal PCB Layout and Grounding Design） 5. Common PCB Grounding Mistakes and Solutions Conclusion There is no single grounding method that works for every PCB layout . Single-point grounding is suitable for some low-frequency sensitive circuits, multi-point grounding is often used where low-impedance high-frequency return paths are required, and mixed grounding combines strategies according to the needs of different circuit sections. In practical PCB layout, prioritize ground-plane continuity, current-loop design, common impedance, and signal return paths. Use IC datasheets, reference designs, and test results to guide design decisions. A well-planned grounding strategy can help reduce noise coupling, improve signal integrity, and enhance overall PCB stability. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing by: Mila Sep 16,2025 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb layout design schematic design pcb layout services pcb layout design services PCB layout design is the process of transforming an electrical schematic into a complete, manufacturable printed circuit board (PCB). A well-designed PCB layout must do more than simply connect components. It needs to balance electrical performance, signal integrity, power integrity, thermal management, mechanical constraints, manufacturability, and reliability. For complex electronic products, decisions made during PCB layout can have a significant impact on product performance, production yield, cost, and time to market. A professional PCB layout workflow therefore requires systematic planning, engineering review, design verification, and manufacturing preparation. Below is an overview of the PCB layout design process we follow, from the initial schematic review to final manufacturing data.You can also find more information on our PCB Layout page . Step 1 – Design Preparation and Engineering Review The PCB layout process begins with a detailed review of the design requirements and source files. Before starting the layout, our engineers review the schematic and project specifications to make sure the design is ready for PCB implementation. This includes checking: Schematic completeness and connectivity Component information and footprints Board dimensions and mechanical constraints Layer count and stack-up requirements Component placement restrictions High-speed and differential signals Power distribution requirements Impedance-control requirements Thermal considerations Manufacturing capabilities and design rules If the customer only provides a PDF or image-based schematic, we can recreate the schematic in professional EDA software before proceeding with PCB layout. If the original schematic file is available, we can directly import the design data, generate the netlist, and establish the PCB design environment. At this stage, we also identify potential design issues that could affect layout, manufacturing, or product performance. Resolving these issues early helps reduce design iterations later in the process. Step 2 – PCB Stack-Up and Design Rule Setup Before component placement and routing, the PCB layer structure and key design rules need to be established. For multilayer and high-speed PCBs, the stack-up directly affects signal integrity, impedance control, power integrity, EMI performance, and manufacturability. Depending on the application, we may define: Number of PCB layers Core and prepreg materials Copper thickness Dielectric thickness Controlled impedance requirements Power and ground reference planes Minimum trace width and spacing Via structures and drill sizes Manufacturing constraints For high-speed designs, impedance-controlled traces and their reference planes are considered from the beginning rather than being treated as an afterthought. The design rules are then configured in the EDA software to ensure that the layout remains consistent with both the electrical requirements and the PCB manufacturer's manufacturing capabilities. Step 3 – Component Placement Component placement is one of the most important stages of PCB layout because it establishes the physical structure of the entire board. The placement strategy typically starts with components whose locations are constrained by the mechanical design, such as: Connectors Switches and buttons Mounting holes Displays Mechanical interfaces Heat sinks and other thermal components Core components such as MCUs, CPUs, FPGAs, memory devices, power ICs, and communication ICs are then positioned according to signal flow, functional relationships, and electrical requirements. Supporting components are placed close to their corresponding devices to minimize unnecessary routing length and improve electrical performance. During placement, we consider several factors simultaneously: Signal Integrity High-speed interfaces and sensitive signals require appropriate component relationships and short, well-controlled routing paths. Power Integrity Decoupling capacitors should be positioned close to the relevant power pins, while power distribution paths should be kept short and low impedance. Thermal Management Heat-generating components need sufficient copper area, thermal vias, airflow consideration, and appropriate spacing from temperature-sensitive devices. EMI/EMC Performance Sensitive analog circuits, high-speed digital circuits, switching power supplies, and other potential noise sources need to be appropriately positioned to reduce interference. Manufacturability Component spacing, assembly orientation, soldering requirements, and accessibility for inspection and rework are also considered. A well-planned placement makes subsequent routing more efficient while improving the overall reliability and manufacturability of the PCB. Step 4 – PCB Routing Once the component placement is finalized, the next stage is PCB routing. Routing is not simply about finding a path between two pads. The routing strategy must consider electrical performance, signal integrity, power distribution, EMI/EMC, and manufacturing constraints. Depending on the design, routing priorities may include: High-Speed and Critical Signals High-speed interfaces such as USB, DDR, PCIe, Ethernet, HDMI, LVDS, and other differential interfaces may require: Controlled impedance Differential-pair routing Length matching Skew control Appropriate reference planes Minimized discontinuities Careful via transitions Critical signals are routed according to their electrical requirements rather than simply following the shortest available path. Power and Ground Power distribution networks are designed to provide stable and low-impedance power delivery. Ground planes are carefully maintained to provide appropriate return paths and reduce unwanted noise and electromagnetic interference. General Signals After critical nets have been addressed, general signal routing is completed according to the defined design rules for: Trace width Trace spacing Via size Clearance Routing layers Manufacturing limitations For dense boards, routing may require multiple iterations of placement and routing optimization to achieve a balance between electrical performance and manufacturability. Step 5– Layout Optimization and Verification After routing is completed, the PCB layout undergoes a detailed optimization and verification process. This stage may include: Copper Pour and Plane Optimization Copper pours and power/ground planes are optimized to improve current return paths, grounding, shielding, and thermal performance. Silkscreen Optimization Reference designators, polarity markings, pin-1 indicators, and other assembly information are adjusted to improve readability and prevent interference with pads or other components. Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Guidelines for Better Soldering Quality PCB Layout Guidelines for Better Soldering Quality by: Mila Nov 04,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb Layout pcb soldering pcb assembly pcb design guidelines PCB design plays an important role in soldering quality and overall assembly reliability. From component placement and pad design to fiducial marks and copper connections, even small layout details can affect solder paste printing, component placement, and reflow soldering. In this article, we'll explore key PCB layout guidelines to help reduce common soldering defects and improve SMT assembly efficiency. Factors Affecting PCB Soldering Quality Producing a high-quality PCB assembly involves multiple stages, from PCB design to component soldering. It requires coordination among PCB designers, process engineers, and production personnel. Several factors can affect PCB soldering quality, including PCB design files, board quality, component quality, oxidation on component leads, solder paste quality, solder paste printing accuracy, pick-and-place programming and placement accuracy, and the reflow oven temperature profile. Among these factors, PCB layout is one of the important elements that directly influence downstream assembly processes. PCB designers may have limited hands-on soldering and manufacturing experience, while production operators at assembly facilities are generally more focused on manufacturing tasks than on analyzing PCB design decisions. If manufacturing and soldering requirements are not considered during the design stage, unnecessary production difficulties may arise. Therefore, PCB designers should consider assembly processes and manufacturing requirements from the beginning to minimize potential problems during production. PCB Design Considerations for Better Soldering The following guidelines cover practical PCB layout considerations that can help reduce soldering defects and improve SMT assembly and repair efficiency. 1. Tooling Holes For PCBs that require SMT assembly, tooling holes can be added according to the requirements of the production equipment. They help secure and position the board during solder paste printing and subsequent manufacturing processes. Tooling holes are generally placed near the board corners or on the tooling edges. When multiple holes are used, their relative positions and machining accuracy should be carefully controlled to avoid positioning errors during production. The number, diameter, and location of tooling holes should be determined based on the PCB dimensions, panelization method, and equipment requirements. Four tooling holes at the corners are not mandatory for every PCB. 2. Fiducial Marks Fiducial marks should be provided on the PCB when required by the SMT equipment. They allow the pick-and-place machine to recognize the board's position and orientation through its vision system, improving component placement accuracy. Fiducial marks are commonly placed diagonally across the PCB and typically use circular exposed copper patterns. Sufficient clearance should be maintained around each mark to prevent nearby copper, pads, or silkscreen graphics from interfering with visual recognition. For double-sided SMT assembly, fiducial marks may be required on both sides, depending on the equipment and assembly process. For panelized PCBs, additional fiducial marks can also be placed on the tooling edges or panel to help the machine identify the entire panel. 3. Fiducial Mark Design Requirements When designing fiducial marks, consider the following points: a. Fiducial marks generally use solid circular exposed copper patterns. Their shape and dimensions should meet the requirements of the pick-and-place machine. b. A typical fiducial mark diameter is approximately 1.0 mm, although the exact size should follow the equipment manufacturer's specifications. c. Maintain a sufficient clearance around each fiducial mark. Avoid placing copper features, pads, silkscreen, or other patterns within this area. A clearance of approximately 1.0 mm around the mark is commonly used, subject to equipment requirements. d. The fiducial mark should provide sufficient contrast against the surrounding PCB surface to ensure reliable visual recognition. e. Keep the fiducial surface clean and flat. Oxidation, contamination, or excessive reflection may affect recognition accuracy. Exposed copper is commonly used, with the surface finish selected according to the PCB manufacturing process. Note that simple silkscreen outlines should not be used as substitutes for fiducial marks. Pick-and-place machines need to recognize a physical feature with a clearly defined boundary and optical characteristics. 4. Maintain Sufficient Clearance from PCB Edges PCB layouts should account for the conveying and clamping requirements of SMT equipment. For boards transported along conveyor rails, sufficient component-free space should be maintained near the board edges to prevent components from interfering with the rails or fixtures. Depending on the equipment, a clearance of approximately 3–5 mm from the board edge may be used as a reference. Avoid placing SMD components, protruding pads, or other features that may interfere with board handling in this area. For double-sided SMT assembly, also consider the risk of component movement or falling during the second reflow process, as well as potential interference between components and conveyor rails. If the PCB is too small to provide sufficient edge clearance, consider adding tooling edges to provide space for board transportation, positioning, and clamping. 5. Avoid Placing Vias Directly in Solder Pads Without Proper Treatment If an untreated via is placed directly within a conventional SMD pad, molten solder may flow into the via during reflow soldering. This can result in insufficient solder at the joint and, in severe cases, lead to weak or unreliable connections. Therefore, vias should generally be avoided directly within ordinary SMD pads. However, Via-in-Pad structures may be necessary for high-density layouts or specific component packages. In such cases, processes such as resin filling and copper capping can be used to prevent solder loss. 6. Polarity Markings for Diodes and Tantalum Capacitors Polarized components, such as diodes and tantalum capacitors, should have clearly defined polarity markings on the PCB to prevent incorrect placement during assembly or manual soldering. Polarity indicators must match the pin definitions in the component datasheet. Standard industry symbols should be used whenever possible. Even when PCB space is limited, ensure that polarity markings remain visible and are not covered by component bodies or other silkscreen graphics. 7. Silkscreen and Component Identification PCB silkscreen should be clear and concise. Avoid excessive component models, specifications, and other text that may make the board difficult to read, especially in high-density layouts. Component reference designators, such as R1, C1, and U1, should be retained whenever possible. They help production personnel identify component locations and make inspection and repair easier. Do not use component descriptions or part numbers without reference designators. This may increase the difficulty of pick-and-place programming and component identification during production. In addition, silkscreen text should not be too small. Place characters away from vias, pads, and other features that may interfere with readability. 8. IC Pad Length For IC packages with exposed leads, such as SOP, PLCC, and QFP, pad length should be determined based on the component lead dimensions and recommended footprint design. Appropriate pad dimensions help ensure proper solder paste printing, solder wetting, and reliable joint formation. They can also provide sufficient access for manual soldering and rework. However, using a fixed ratio, such as 1.5 times the IC lead length, is not recommended as a universal rule. Different package types have different lead structures and dimensions. Always refer to the recommended land pattern in the component datasheet or relevant IPC footprint design guidelines. 9. IC Pad Width For IC packages such as SOP, PLCC, and QFP, pad width and the spacing between adjacent pads directly affect soldering quality. Follow the recommended footprint dimensions in the component datasheet when determining pad width and spacing. Pads that are too wide or have insufficient spacing between them may increase the risk of solder bridging during assembly. For fine-pitch IC packages in particular, careful attention should be paid to pad dimensions, solder paste printing accuracy, and solder mask design. 10. Avoid Arbitrary Component Rotation During PCB layout, pay attention to component orientation and rotation angles. Keeping components of the same type oriented consistently can simplify pick-and-place programming, inspection, and maintenance. It is worth noting that modern pick-and-place machines generally support arbitrary component rotation angles and are not limited to 90°, 180°, or 270° increments. However, component rotation must be consistent with the footprint definition, coordinate files, and placement program. Otherwise, component leads may become misaligned with PCB pads, affecting placement and soldering quality. Pay particular attention to polarity when positioning diodes, electrolytic capacitors, and other polarized components. 11. Connecting Adjacent IC Pins When adjacent IC pins need to be electrically connected, the PCB layout should be designed carefully to avoid soldering problems and make inspection easier. Avoid simply merging multiple pad areas into one large copper region. Instead, use appropriate routing connections and solder mask openings according to the electrical requirements. Ensure that the soldering areas of individual pins remain clearly defined. Sufficient clearance must be maintained between pads that should not be electrically connected to prevent solder bridging. 12. Exposed Thermal Pads Under IC Packages Some IC packages, such as QFN and DFN, have an exposed thermal pad on the underside of the component. This pad is mainly used for heat dissipation and electrical grounding. When designing these packages, follow the recommended thermal pad dimensions in the component datasheet and consider the solder paste stencil design. If the thermal pad is too large and the entire area is covered with solder paste, excessive solder paste may cause problems such as solder voiding, component floating, or solder overflow during reflow. To reduce these risks, the solder paste opening can be divided into multiple smaller sections to control the amount of solder paste deposited. However, the thermal pad should not be arbitrarily reduced simply to prevent short circuits. Thermal performance, electrical connections, and soldering requirements must all be considered. 13. Avoid Placing Two Tall Components Too Close Together Component height and spacing should be considered during PCB layout. If two tall components are placed too close together, the pick-and-place machine may encounter interference when positioning the second component. The first component may obstruct the placement head or nozzle, affecting the placement process. Overcrowded layouts can also make inspection, soldering, and rework more difficult. Therefore, consider component height, package dimensions, nozzle clearance, and maintenance requirements when arranging taller components. Provide sufficient spacing to avoid mechanical interference. 14. BGA Design Considerations BGA components have solder balls underneath the package. Since these solder joints cannot be directly inspected from the outside after assembly, BGA packages require careful attention to PCB pad design, solder paste printing, and reflow soldering. When designing BGA footprints, strictly follow the component datasheet recommendations for pad dimensions, ball pitch, and PCB layout requirements. It is also important to consider inspection and rework requirements in advance. For example, additional positioning features may be needed on the PCB to accommodate BGA rework equipment and fixtures. If auxiliary tooling holes are required, their diameter, location, and spacing should match the actual rework equipment or alignment fixture. A single hole size should not be applied to every BGA design. 15. PCB Solder Mask Color Although solder mask color does not directly determine soldering quality, it may affect the visual recognition performance of SMT equipment. Different solder mask colors have different optical and reflective characteristics, which may influence how the machine's vision system recognizes fiducial marks and component positions. For example, certain dark solder mask colors may provide insufficient contrast under specific lighting conditions. Therefore, when selecting a PCB color, consider not only appearance but also compatibility with the production equipment's vision system. For unusual solder mask colors, confirm compatibility with the PCB manufacturer and SMT assembly provider in advance. 16. Small Components Under Large Components During PCB layout, avoid placing small components underneath large components when doing so may obstruct soldering, inspection, or rework. For example, if resistors or capacitors are placed underneath a seven-segment display or a large connector, technicians may need to remove the larger component before repairing the smaller one if a soldering defect occurs. This increases repair complexity and may damage the larger component or nearby pads during removal. Therefore, when circuit functionality and routing requirements allow, consider placing some small components on the opposite side of the PCB or repositioning them to provide better access for inspection and repair. 17. How Copper Pour Connections Affect Soldering When a PCB pad is directly connected to a large copper pour, heat may dissipate more rapidly during soldering. This can slow down pad heating and affect solder melting and wetting. This is particularly relevant for pads connected to large copper planes or internal power and ground layers. For example, in Figure A, the component pad is directly connected to a large copper area. In Figure B, although the connector pad is not directly connected to the copper pour, the large copper planes in the inner layers may still increase the overall thermal mass and affect soldering. If the reflow temperature is increased to compensate for excessive heat dissipation, temperature-sensitive connectors or plastic components may become deformed. Therefore, for pads that do not require direct high-current connections or special thermal performance, consider using thermal relief connections. These connections use narrow copper spokes to reduce heat dissipation and improve solderability. For high-current pads and thermal pads, however, current-carrying capacity, heat dissipation, and soldering requirements must be considered together. Thermal relief should not be applied indiscriminately. 18. PCB Panelization and Tooling Edge Design For small or irregularly shaped PCBs, panelization can improve SMT production efficiency by allowing multiple boards to be processed together. Several factors should be considered when designing PCB panels: Tooling Edge: Add tooling edges according to the conveying and clamping requirements of SMT equipment. This provides sufficient space for automated assembly. Fiducial Marks: Place fiducial marks on individual boards and the panel when required by the equipment to ensure accurate positioning. Tooling Holes: Add tooling holes as needed to keep the panel stable during manufacturing and assembly. Breakaway Methods: Select an appropriate separation method, such as V-scoring or mouse bites, based on the PCB structure and depanelization requirements. Component Clearance: Maintain sufficient clearance between components and separation areas to prevent mechanical stress from damaging components or solder joints during depanelization. A well-designed PCB panel can improve SMT production efficiency while reducing positioning errors and mechanical damage during assembly. Conclusion PCB layout should consider not only circuit functionality and electrical performance but also downstream manufacturing, soldering, inspection, and repair requirements. Proper fiducial mark placement, pad design, component arrangement, and panelization can help reduce potential problems during solder paste printing, SMT placement, and reflow soldering.
